items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's remind ourselves of the first few powers of [MATH: \textrm{i}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{i}^{1}|= \textrm{i}; \textrm{i}^{2}|= − 1; \textrm{i}^{3}|= − \textrm{i}; \textrm{i}^{4}|= 1]

Content:
At the fourth power, we return to the value of [MATH: 1,] which can also be written as [MATH: \textrm{i}^0 = 1.] This means that if we continue to increase the powers, we would cycle through the same four values once again, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fbffb9f09d2e7822b179e42e2c24ea85]

Content:
So, for [MATH: \textrm{i}^5] through [MATH: \textrm{i}^8,] the exact same pattern repeats. Remembering that [MATH: \textrm{i}^4 = 1,] we have
[MATH: \eqalign{
\textrm{i}^5&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
\textrm{i}^6&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
\textrm{i}^7&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
\textrm{i}^8&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1 .
}]

Content:
Similarly, for [MATH: \textrm{i}^9] through to [MATH: \textrm{i}^{12},] the pattern repeats again:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\textrm{i}^9&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
\textrm{i}^{10}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
\textrm{i}^{11}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
\textrm{i}^{12}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1
}]

Content:
Therefore, to simplify a higher integer power of [MATH: \textrm{i},] we divide the power by [MATH: 4] and raise [MATH: \textrm{i}] to the remainder.

Content:
Let's see this idea in action.

To find the value of [MATH: \textrm{i}] to some positive integer power [MATH: n], we divide [MATH: n] by [MATH: 4] and raise [MATH: \textrm{i}] to the remainder.

In our case, we have [MATH: n=15.] Dividing the power by [MATH: 4,] we get

[MATH: 15\div 4 = 3\,\textrm{R} \color{blue}{3}.]

So the remainder is [MATH: \color{blue}3.] Therefore,

[MATH: \textrm{i}^{15} = \textrm{i}^{\color{blue}{3}} = -\textrm{i}.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Cyclic Nature of Powers of i

Content:
Let's remind ourselves of the first few powers of [MATH: \textrm{i}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{i}^{1}|= \textrm{i}; \textrm{i}^{2}|= − 1; \textrm{i}^{3}|= − \textrm{i}; \textrm{i}^{4}|= 1]

Content:
At the fourth power, we return to the value of [MATH: 1,] which can also be written as [MATH: \textrm{i}^0 = 1.] This means that if we continue to increase the powers, we would cycle through the same four values once again, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fbffb9f09d2e7822b179e42e2c24ea85]

Content:
So, for [MATH: \textrm{i}^5] through [MATH: \textrm{i}^8,] the exact same pattern repeats. Remembering that [MATH: \textrm{i}^4 = 1,] we have
[MATH: \eqalign{
\textrm{i}^5&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
\textrm{i}^6&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
\textrm{i}^7&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
\textrm{i}^8&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1 .
}]

Content:
Similarly, for [MATH: \textrm{i}^9] through to [MATH: \textrm{i}^{12},] the pattern repeats again:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\textrm{i}^9&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
\textrm{i}^{10}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
\textrm{i}^{11}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
\textrm{i}^{12}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1
}]

Content:
Therefore, to simplify a higher integer power of [MATH: \textrm{i},] we divide the power by [MATH: 4] and raise [MATH: \textrm{i}] to the remainder.

Content:
Let's see this idea in action.
